summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for remote network monitoring. It describes objects that monitoring devices, called probes, keep so a management station can collect statistics and watch network traffic. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2819 defines SNMP objects that a remote probe uses to monitor a network and report information to a management station. The probe can keep collecting data, raise alarms and save packets while the station is away.

questions: what groups are in the rmon mib
how do rmon alarms and thresholds work
subtitle: The SNMP management objects a remote probe uses to collect statistics, create alarms and capture packets.

tldr.problem: A network manager may need statistics and packet information from a remote network segment even when the management station cannot stay connected to the monitoring device.
tldr.mechanism: The Remote Network Monitoring Management Information Base (RMON MIB) defines optional groups of SNMP objects. A probe collects statistics, keeps history, tracks hosts and conversations, checks thresholds, filters traffic and captures packets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2819 republishes the RMON MIB in SMIv2 format while remaining semantically identical to RFC 1757. It is an Internet Standard, STD 59.

today: RFC 2819 is an Internet Standard (STD 59) and obsoletes RFC 1757. It has no later updates listed in the work-unit metadata.

sections.title: What a Remote Monitoring Probe Does
sections.content:
Remote Network Monitoring devices, often called probes or monitors, collect and analyze information on a network segment. The management station reads their objects through SNMP; the objects are an interface for management software, not a set of values intended for people to edit by hand.

The RFC's goals include offline operation, proactive monitoring, problem detection and reporting, useful summary data, and support for multiple management stations. A probe can continue collecting statistics even when its management station cannot reach it.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe watches a network and records what it sees, even when the management station is disconnected. The station can later read those records and check for problems.

sections.title: The Ten Optional RMON Groups
sections.content:
The MIB organizes objects into ten groups: Ethernet statistics, history control, Ethernet history, alarms, hosts, HostTopN, matrices, filters, packet capture and events. Each group is optional, but an implementation that claims a group must implement all of its objects. A probe implementing the MIB must also implement the MIB-II system group and IF-MIB.

The groups cover different questions. They count traffic and errors, save periodic samples, identify hosts and conversations, select packets with filters, capture matching packets, and record or notify about events.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has groups for counts, history, alarms, hosts, conversations, filters, packet captures and events. A probe can choose which groups it supports, but it must provide a complete group once it claims one.

sections.title: Configuring and Sharing Probe Resources
sections.content:
Many RMON functions use a read-write control table to set parameters and a read-only data table to store results. A control entry may need to be invalidated before its parameters can change; invalidating it also removes associated data and frees resources.

Each management-station-created function has an owner string so managers can identify who is using scarce probe resources. Rows use an EntryStatus value such as createRequest, underCreation, valid or invalid. If managers try to create the same row simultaneously, only the first succeeds.
sections.plainLanguage: Managers configure a probe through control entries, and the probe stores results separately. Owner labels help several managers recognize who created each job and avoid competing for the same resources.

sections.title: Threshold Alarms and Events
sections.content:
The alarm group samples a numeric variable and compares it with rising and falling thresholds. It can compare the current value directly or compare the change since the previous sample. When a threshold is crossed, the alarm can trigger an event.

Hysteresis prevents repeated alarms while a value remains on one side of a threshold. After a rising event, another rising event waits until the value falls and reaches the falling threshold; after a falling event, it waits until the value rises to the rising threshold. Events can be logged, sent as SNMP traps, both, or neither.
sections.plainLanguage: An alarm checks a value against upper and lower limits. It rings once when a limit is crossed, then waits for the value to cross the other limit before ringing again.

sections.title: Hosts, Conversations and Captured Packets
sections.content:
The host group records statistics for MAC addresses seen in good packets. HostTopN reports the hosts with the highest rates for a selected statistic, and the matrix group keeps statistics for conversations between address pairs.

The filter group matches packets and creates channels from matching traffic. The packet capture group saves packets that pass through a channel. On Ethernet, the RFC defines good packets as error-free frames from 64 through 1518 octets; captured packet contents may include sensitive user information.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe can count traffic by host, identify busy hosts and record which addresses communicate. Filters can select packets for capture or trigger events.

sections.title: SMIv2 Format and Security
sections.content:
RFC 2819 expresses the MIB in Structure of Management Information version 2 (SMIv2). The RFC says an SMIv1 translation can be semantically equivalent, except where objects such as Counter64 cannot be translated. This version obsoletes RFC 1757 and reformats the module.

A probe analyzes packets between third parties, and packet capture can expose user data or passwords. The RFC recommends restricting SNMP access to sensitive read and write operations and advises implementers to consider SNMPv3's User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control Model.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC rewrites the earlier MIB in a newer description format while keeping its meaning. Because probes can see packet contents, only authorized managers should be able to read captures or change probe settings.

items.title: Statistics and history
items.text: Counts traffic and keeps periodic samples.

items.title: Alarms and events
items.text: Checks thresholds, logs events or sends traps.

items.title: Hosts and matrices
items.text: Tracks host activity and address-pair conversations.

items.title: Filters and capture
items.text: Selects traffic and stores matching packets.
